utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 11th of March, 2009. I'd like to greet all the accused who are sitting in this courtroom, the attorneys, Defence counsel, representatives of the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom. As you know, we will hear one witness and then another witness. Hamid Bahto is the first witness. The Defence has said that it would need 30 minutes. The Trial Chamber, therefore, allocates 15 minutes for the cross-examination of the other Defence counsel and allocates 30 minutes for the cross-examination of the OTP. As far as the second witness is concerned, the Defence has stipulated that it would need 45 minutes. Therefore, the Trial Chamber grants the other Defence counsel 23 minutes and the OTP 45 minutes. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom now. Registrar, I think you have four IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted its objections to documents tendered by 2D and 4D through witness Dragan Pinjuh. These objections shall be given Exhibit IC943 and 944, respectively. Two parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through witness Majic, Tihomir. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC945. And the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC946. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you state your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Hamid Bahto. I was born on the 3rd of January, 1961, Rogatica municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, are you currently occupied [as interpreted] and do you have a job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been retired from the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I was a general of the BH Army and retired in 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, have you already testified in a trial on those events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time you come to testify today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first time that I'm testifying about the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to take the oath and read the text of the solemn declaration which the usher will show you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, some brief information. As Ms. Nozica has told you, you will be asked to answer a number of questions, and you will have a look at a number of documents. I believe there are six documents which she will show you. After that, the Defence counsel of the other accused, since Ms. Nozica represents Mr. Stojic, may also put questions to you as part of their cross-examination, after which the OTP, sitting on your right-hand side, will also put questions to you and will have the same time as Ms. Nozica. The four Judges that form the Bench may also step in at any time and put you some questions. Please try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer. If you don't understand the meaning of a sentence, please ask the person who put it to you to rephrase it. We have a break every hour and a half. If you have a problem at any stage, please let us know, and then we will adjourn and you can have a rest. This is what I wanted to tell you to make sure that your testimony runs as smoothly as possible. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom, and good afternoon to you, too, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read out briefly some important points concerning your CV, and you'll just tell me if what I'm reading out is correct. You graduated from the Faculty of Political Sciences in 1985 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In 1991, you were appointed commander of the TO, that is to say, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Maybe it would be better if I were to read the CV out, and then at the end you can tell me whether I've read it out correctly. So you were appointed TO commander of the Civilian Protection Staff, and a professional associate to train civilian structures in the Stari Grad municipality of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, 1992, you became commander of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Stari Grad municipality, Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And from that time until the end of the war, you performed various duties within the BH Army. In 2005, you retired, and you have the rank of general of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that information correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, the information is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bahto, I know from the proofing session, and since we've known each other for quite some time, I know that you tend to answer and speak quickly, but because everything I say and all your answers have to be recorded in the transcript, I'd like to ask you to make brief pauses between my question and your answer. Mr. Bahto, what assignments did you have at the beginning of 1992, because we have seen that at the time or, rather, as of April, you were the commander of the Municipal Staff of the TO of Sarajevo, so I'm asking you now what were your first tasks and assignments?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: At the time, I was working in the Municipal Assembly of Stari Grad, Sarajevo. I worked in the Secretariat for National Defence, and I was commander of the Staff for Civilian Protection, and I worked with the training of civilians in the defence area. So in keeping with that role of mine, I had the task of, from 1991 to the beginning of 1992, as commander of the Civilian Protection Staff, preparing all the shelters and civilian defence units, special-purpose units, units for special purposes within the Civilian Defence Sector, to activate the NUS, and to prepare all the staffs and the population in general for the burgeoning aggression which at that time was already being exerted against the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia. And that role of mine I performed right up until the 6th of April, when I was appointed commander of the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence. And in the meantime, while I was performing the work of commander, I was also a member of the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Stari Grad municipality, which, establishment-wise, is a duty that I would do by virtue of my position, and automatically I would become a member of the Crisis Staff engaged in preparations to stand up to the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's clarify matters first. You said the aggression started in Slovenia and Croatia before. Aggression from whom?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: From the Yugoslav People's Army and the vestiges of the former Yugoslavia or, rather, the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro, which were a component part of the rump Yugoslavia, and the Yugoslav People's Army which was under their command. That means the Yugoslav People's Army had launched an aggression against the then Republic of Slovenia and Croatia, and at that time, I have to clarify here, an aggression had been launched, in part, against Bosnia and Herzegovina already in 1991, from the month of September. The Army of Yugoslavia used the sovereign territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina to attack Croatia, the village of Ravno, Brcko, and so on. They'd already entered that territory and taken control of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the task of this Crisis Staff of yours of Stari Grad municipality? What was one of its prime tasks?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: One of its prime tasks was to prepare ourselves; to prepare for the mobilisation of the Civilian Protection units and Territorial Defence units, to replenish the numbers, to have the necessary shelters where people could take refuge, and to start forming the units themselves, units for defence, that is, and to start arming those units and the crisis staffs that would set them up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you take part directly in the procurement of weapons, as the president of the Crisis Staff? Did you take part in any activities like that?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I directly took part. I wasn't the president of the Crisis Staff, but I was a member of the Crisis Staff, because, ex officio, the mayor was the president of the Crisis Staff, the presidents of the municipalities, whereas the commander of the Civilian Protection Staff and the minister of interior, ex officio, would become members of the Crisis Staff. Now, as to my own role --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A little slower, please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I apologise. As I was saying, it was my task to establish the units and to try and find the equipment and weapons that those units needed in order to defend themselves and the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber whether during that time, and we're talking about the beginning of 1992, any weapons existed in the Crisis Staff? Did the crisis staffs have weapons?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1991 and 1992, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have any weaponry, either in the crisis staffs or in the local communes or in the units, because this is what happened: In 1989 and 1990, orders were issued by the Yugoslav Army and the General Staff of the JNA to withdraw all the weapons under the Territorial Defence and to place them in barracks for safekeeping. These orders were carried out up until 1991. Sometime in December -- or November or December of 1990, the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina handed over all their weapons to the JNA for storage, so that the weapons were seized from the socio-political organisations, working units, the Territorial Defence staffs, and all the commands under the Staff Command. So all the weaponry was taken and placed under the command of the JNA, so that Bosnia and Herzegovina was completely disarmed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what about the principal tasks, your principal task in procuring weapons for the units and organs preparing for defence?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Well, the main task was to establish contacts with higher levels of power and authority, that is to say, with the state organs, so that they could try, for their part, to procure weapons for our requirements. The only way -- the only possible way at that time for procuring weapons was to go through the Republic of Croatia and Slovenia, and the Municipal Crisis Staff at the time or, rather, the presidents and their members, wielded their influence on the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina to set up contacts with those two republics in order to procure weapons through them, because it was quite obvious that there were conflicts going on and that there was an aggression being prepared, and we had to act quickly. And we managed to come into contact with our people and with the Croats and Slovenes and started to procure weapons and arm those units of ours which we had already established by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you specifically, did you take part in any operations or activities linked to procuring weapons for your Crisis Staff? And if so, could you explain to the Trial Chamber how you did that?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I did take part, on several occasions, in activities geared towards procuring weapons for the units that I was in command of or, rather, the units that I established and trained and equipped and armed. And sometime at the beginning of 1992, I came into contact with our authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Sarajevo, and I intervened to persuade them to procure a large quantity of weapons for the Stari Grad municipality, because we were in the forefront of the enemy attack. That's where we were most vulnerable. I apologise for speaking so quickly once again. So as we were at the forefront of the attack, the axis of attack, I insisted, with the authorities, that they procure weapons as soon as possible. And after some time had passed, we did indeed receive permission to take over a quantity of weapons, and I was given the specific task of going to Grude, to report there to Tihomir Majic, and from him to take over a quantity of infantry weapons, ammunition and other MTS or materiel and technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bahto, do you know how and with whom -- or, rather, who it was in the political sphere that saw to the procurement of weapons and made the decision?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Well, our political leaders, which was the SDA party, in fact, and the HDZ party, so those two parties, our representatives -- top representatives in those parties agreed with the HDZ party that we should go ahead with arming ourselves, that is to say, between the Muslim and the Croatian people, and they set up contacts -- established contacts with the Republic of Slovenia and took a large quantity -- or, rather, they came into contact with the president of the Republic of Croatia and the president of Slovenia. They reached an agreement, and important quantities of weapons and MTS reached Grude, and from there it was transported throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we're now talking about the weapons that were procured in February 1992, right, and you say that an agreement had been made between the leaders of the Muslim people and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina to procure the weapons. Now, can you tell us specifically who and in what way purchased the arms? Who was in charge of actually purchasing the weapons and doing that -- seeing to that technical side of the whole issue?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: The technical side was done by the representatives of our authorities; President Izetbegovic, in fact, our president. President Izetbegovic reached an agreement with Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Kucan, I believe it was, and the HDZ, and they said that they would procure MTS to be transported to Croatia, and then from Croatia into Bosnia, because at that time Bosnia had already been cut off, blocked. It was in a sort of isolation, so you couldn't have the weapons transported directly to Bosnia-Herzegovina. It went to Western Herzegovina first and then to Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment. I apologise for interrupting, but who bought the weapons? Was it -- do you know who the weapons were bought from and who the purchaser was?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Well, the weapons were purchased from the MUP of the Republic of Slovenia, and it was people from the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia who were in charge of seeing to the transport of the weapons and to having the weapons procured, distributed to the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know who, in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was in charge of that technical side of the business?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Well, on behalf of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was Mr. Alija Delimustafic who was given the task of implementing this with Mr. Bruno Stojic, also from the MUP. The two of them were -- well, Alija Delimustafic and Bruno Stojic, they were in charge, and before that, our representatives agreed all this with Boban. So Boban was the person who assigned the task to Bruno, and our president gave the assignment to Alija Delimustafic, and they went ahead and put that into practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could the witness be given my binder so that we can look at the documents testifying to what the witness has just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like you now to take a look at the first document in that binder. It is 2D1253.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: That's a receipt, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just slowly. Let's have it put up on e-court first so that we can see it all on our screens. I'm going to ask you, Mr. Bahto, if you can explain, using this first example, of whether that is the receipt for the weapons that you've been talking to us about.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is the MTS that I took delivery of from Tihomir Majic at that time, and he was down there in the warehouse in Grude. When I arrived, I took delivery of 1.000 automatic rifles, Kalashnikov, 7.62, 39 rounds, and the ammunition. On the receipt here -- well, actually, I took over -- I took delivery of some more materiel and technical equipment, but they're not included on this receipt, and I was told to send them to Eastern Bosnia, to Foca, and to hand them over to the authorities in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, it says down there at the bottom -- you say you were in the Crisis Staff of Stari Grad. Here, you have your ID number, and it says "Novi Grad." So why does it say "Novi Grad" there?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: It says "Bahto, Hamid." This is my ID card number, 7582/89. At the time, I lived in Novi Grad municipality, Alipasino Polje, and worked in the municipality of Stari Grad, so your ID card had the municipality where you were residing, and that's why it says "Novi Grad."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, at that point in time, were these significant quantities of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, very significant, and the defence of Sarajevo, Stari Grad and the broader region around it depended on these quantities. And this is the first quantity of weaponry brought into Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, would you look at the next receipts that you have in this document, 114 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, one short question. I'm listening to you very carefully, and everything that you are saying is being recorded. You said you brought MTS to Foca. Unfortunately, I don't have the map in front of me. If I had, I could have put a more specific question to you. When you brought the weapons to Foca, for which unit of the ABiH were they designed for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was intended for the defenders of Foca at that time, and they were organised groups at the time. We're talking about 1992. It was the Territorial Defence of Foca, just before the war broke out. And Foca is in the eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, bordering on Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue. The Judge asked you where Foca is, so you can continue there.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: The Foca municipality is located in Eastern Bosnia, about 72 kilometres away from Sarajevo, east of Sarajevo 72 kilometres. It is one of the largest municipalities in Eastern Bosnia, and I was given the task, since it lies on the very border with Montenegro and Serbia, to have those -- that technical equipment sent there, because that's where the attack would come, the attack against sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the map in front of us. Please indicate where Foca is with your pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just mark the border with Montenegro [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I have understood correctly, the weapons you bring to Foca, which you pick up in Grude, are not designed for the Posavina, and are not designed for Sarajevo either, but are to be delivered to Foca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honours, Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The witness's answer is appearing on the screen now. Can we just keep the map where it is. The usher need not stick around. We'll be getting to other locations that the witness will explain at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bahto, could you please now look at the following receipts, and briefly explain to the Trial Chamber who Ramo Calsevic [phoen] is? Ramo Calsevic, all of these receipts, can you please explain if all this was for the defence of the Muslims, because at this point in time there was no BH Army, was there?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Talking of Calsevic, Ramo, the Brcko SUP, this was something for the BH Army. At the time, Croats were also a part of the army. The Muslims and Croats were together, but the majority population was Muslim. The same thing goes for Kupres. All of this is MTS for the BH Army. At the time, it was not the BH Army, it was the crisis staffs and the Territorial Defence. The Army came into existence later, and the TO became the Army. That's when talking about defence, in the generic sense now. The next receipt, Hasim Hodzic, Travnik SDA, the same thing applies; this is for the Muslims and for the Croats in the Central Bosnia canton. Again, the Rifat Burovic receipt, the MTS arrived. It was there. It was received by the BH Army. And the same thing applies to all the other receipts that I can see here up to Bugojno. Dzevad Mlaco, he also took delivery of the MTS that arrived in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be hurrying things along, but we do have a number of other documents to explain. Can you tell me, please, whether you know that all these other persons arrived in Grude the same way as you? They had been invited to go there and take delivery of the weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, the same way as I did. They received at the headquarters, the SDA headquarters over there, a mission, where to go, when to go, and to get the weapons, so it was the same way in which I got there. They got the name of a person. They got the name of a place that they were supposed to go to in order to take delivery of the weapons that had arrived at Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Can we now please go to the next document, 2D00955. It's document number 2 in the binder. We see here we're talking about the 29th of April, 1992. We see that the weapons were received by Enver Backovic. Just very briefly, please, can you explain to the Chamber if you know this person, and was this person, too, involved in supplying weapons to the BH Army for defence purposes?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Talking of Enver Backovic, Enver Backovic is a professor; he has a Ph.D. in economics. He works at the Sarajevo Faculty. He joined the same time as I, before the war in the preparations for defending from the aggression. He was with a number of friends. His brother, Enver, Zagi, who is even more famous than he was, Dr. Rucarevic, they set up certain units that got their weapons in the same way that we did, members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next document, 3D00437. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll ask you a number of questions about this one. The last witness to appear here was asked the same questions. It says here that on the 16th of October -- actually, this is an order from 1992, talking about MTS being distributed to the BH Army and the HVO in Gorazde, Foca, Trnovo, and Visegrad. My first question would be: Were you familiar with the situation in 1992 in this area, what units were there? I'm talking about the 16th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I was well aware of the situation in these areas. This is in Eastern Bosnia. I'm a native of the area. I know by heart each of these towns and villages. Of course, we were more than well aware of the situation in the area. Most of my family were still in the area. I was dispatching weapons to these areas as well, the weapons that I was receiving in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know of any HVO units existing in Gorazde, Foca, Trnovo, and Visegrad at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: At the time, and generally speaking throughout the war, there were no Croats in Eastern Bosnia. Therefore, there were no Croatian units there, with one exception. There was a Croatian unit that was not part of the HVO, but part of the HOS, H-O-S, and that unit was in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The HOS unit, H-O-S, was under the command of the BH Army, right?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, it was under the command of the commander of the East Bosnia Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bahto, another question in relation to this document. Do you know Senad Hasimbakic [as interpreted]? His name is handwritten on this document.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, I know Senad Sahinpasic. I know him well. We're friends and neighbours. This is a man who used a Croatian connection to supply weapons and equipment to the BH Army units in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We don't have the family name on the transcript, but we'll deal with that later. Now 3D436. Can you please just confirm -- the date is the 10th of October, 1992. Briefly, please, do you know if these weapons, too, were used for the purposes of Foca and Gorazde, I mean, the BH Army? 3D436. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These units from Eastern Bosnia that at the time were called the Eastern Bosnia Operations Group, had a logistics HQ near Sarajevo called Grebak. All the material on equipment that came through Croatia and through Grude, whether from Metkovic or from Grude, would normally reach the Grebak base. Then one would carry this on to Gorazde, over a distance of 50 kilometres, on horseback, or they would just walk there with the equipment. All of the MTS and equipment would arrive at this base, and from there people would walk, carry the equipment and weapons on their backs, to Gorazde. Just in order to explain, to make this perfectly clear, Gorazde was among these municipalities in Eastern Bosnia, Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, Gorazde, Foca, and Pale Praca. These were municipalities that were under the command of the commander of the East Bosnia Operations Group. They were sealed off from the rest of the front-line. They were isolated. The only way to get supplies through to them was to actually walk there from the Grebak base and physically carry the supplies there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please get on with the other two documents. The next two documents would be the following: 2D311. We see MTS being issued here to the BH Army through the Grude Logistics Base. The next document, please, 2D -- or, rather, I'm sorry, 3D008, 3D008. Are you familiar with the name of Seta Suajb? That's what's written here. Who is that person mentioned in both of these documents?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Seta Suajb, his real name is Suajb, he's a high-ranking officer of the BH Army. He is now serving with the BH Army. At the time, he was a logistics officer at the Zagreb base. His mission there was to dispatch supplies to the BH Army units, in terms of weapons and equipment, of course, from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Can you tell me this: If these weapons, as these two documents state, were dispatched to the armed forces of the BH Army, can you in that case explain to the Chamber what the Logistics Base at Visoko was exactly? Was that a central logistics base from which supplies were dispatched for the whole BH Army?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Talking about the Visoko base, its name was GLOC, Main Logistics Centre of the BH Army, that's what the abbreviation stood for. The task of that base was to make sure supplies were available for all the BH Army units, in terms of materiel, in terms of equipment, weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Visoko is? And then you can explain to the Chamber, by using the map that you have there.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Visoko is right next to Sarajevo [indicates]. Visoko is a municipality near Sarajevo, the distance between the two being 28 kilometres, to the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about the Visoko area? Were there any HVO forces nearby, and did the HVO units get any supplies whatsoever from this base?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Visoko or -- rather, the Visoko municipality borders on predominantly Croat municipalities, such as Kiseljak and all the other ones. I can't say specifically, but I don't think the HVO units got any supplies from that base, at least not as far as I know. There is a possibility, however, that they did get supplies from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Bahto, to the best of your knowledge, did the BH Army get supplies throughout the war either from Croatia, through HZ-HB territory, or directly from Croatia? Could the BH Army get any supplies in any other way from other territories?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: The BH Army got their supplies in the following way: They could either, directly or indirectly, get supplies from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and that's what happened. They got their supplies directly from the Republic of Croatia, the 5th Corps, over in the Krajina area, and indirectly the Logistics Base in Visoko, through all the municipalities that were under the control of the Croats, the HVO, meaning directly or across territories under the control of the HVO. Our units, they got their weapons, their food, their ammunition, and all the other supplies from there. All the MTS, weapons, equipment, and other such items, had to come from Croatia across Croat-held territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's how they got to the Central Logistics Base. There is something else that I have to mention here. The territories under the control of the BH Army could not all get their supplies from the Logistics Base, the Main Logistics Base. Therefore, the Eastern Bosnia Operations Group had to get their supplies directly through Grude, Grebak and Gorazde; whereas the units under the 1st Corps, the 2nd Corps, the 3rd Corps, and the 4th Corps got their supplies through Western Herzegovina, through Grude, and then on to Metkovic, further south, and then across Kiseljak, Visoko, Kakanj, Vares, what do I know, through Tuzla, Zenica, and that's how they, I mean, got their, I mean, supply, I mean, the BH Army units. I mean, it all had to go through Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Bahto. I think my time is up. This was examination-in-chief. Thank you for all your answers, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have two short questions for you following the examination-in-chief, but these are accessory questions. You were a member of the ABiH, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The accused here in the dock, those two generals among them, were they enemies to you? What did they represent, on the ground, in 1993 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I mean, the leadership -- I mean, the top leadership of the HDZ and their top-most leaders at the time, I didn't, I mean, imagine that -- I couldn't possibly imagine that we were enemies, that we were facing off in this conflict, the reason being, I mean, the MTS during the war, all of them, I mean, I got through them. So they had to be -- there had to be some sort of consent on their part for them to supply all these to us. However, your question is a double-edged sword. There were clashes between the BH Army and the HVO. I wasn't directly involved in that. I was, I mean, facing, I mean, the Serbs, or, rather, the Army of Yugoslavia. My area of responsibility was Romanija, Eastern Bosnia, and, I mean, all the way up to Foca. There were, I mean, units of the former Yugoslav Army there and the Army of Republika Srpska. And, I mean, when I was transferred to the General Staff, I mean, I had contacts with members of the HVO, and at the time while I was there we had contacts with them. We cooperated, we made agreements, and we used each other's help about getting weapons, about preparing for combat, about reconnaissance. Nevertheless, the local commander in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the HVO, for whatever reasons, triggered these clashes. It was all partial and only local. It wasn't throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina; some areas, yes, and some areas, no, in terms of hostile atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already answered the next question I was about to ask you. We know that there was a whole series of conflicts between the ABiH and the HVO. No need to repeat them, because everybody is aware of them. We understood that you were mainly focused on the Serbs. However, at your level then, you left the army being a general, regarding the conflicts between the ABiH and the HVO, I understood, and you repeated it, that these were conflicts between local commanders; is that what you said earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how it was. They were conflicts between local commanders. For example, the 4th Operative Zone of Orasje, the 2nd Corps, they were all joint units, the HVO and the BH Army together, the 107th Brigade, and then Gradacac, numbering 1200 men. Throughout the war, they fought together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may not be able to answer my following question. When the ABiH attacked the HVO in Bugojno, in Vares, were they local conflicts, according to you, or were they conflicts of a different scale or scope?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were conflicts of a local character. Vares is a small municipality, you see, which at the time was insignificant. Now, why a conflict broke out there, I was never quite clear on that, but it was a local conflict. It wasn't an all-out conflict in Posavina, Bihac, or anything like that, or down in Herzegovina, or around Sarajevo; just in those two municipalities, those two areas, those two areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. Your answers express your point of view, or is that also the view shared by all of the officers in the ABiH; for instance, by General Delic, or by General Halilovic? What you have just said, is that your personal point of view or is that a general feeling you've just expressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, well, it's my opinion, and I think that the majority of the BH Army leadership shared that view. They were all local conflicts. During one period of time, the initial period of the war, we were together, the end of the war together, so except for the middle in 1993 and 1994. Otherwise, all local.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you are the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my client, General Praljak, would like to ask two or three direct questions, if you would permit. Certainly, he would understand that those are limited questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are these questions of military nature, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For us to be able to understand this question around Eastern Bosnia, Foca, Gorazde and so on, tell the Judges what happened in the area to the Muslim population in World War II? From the aspects of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, why was it important to send --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, what is the relevance of events that took place 50 years earlier? That's the question that the Trial Chamber has in mind. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Highly relevant, Your Honour, and people remember. There is something that we refer to as the people's memory, and that influences where the weapons were sent and what the people remember, what the state of their soul was like. So the General, who's from the area, can tell us the people's state of mind and also tell us what happened 45 years previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer. Can I? General Praljak asked a very good question, and it is cause and effect, mutually linked. In 1941 or, rather, between 1941 and 1945 -- or, rather, in 1941, the overall Muslim population were slaughtered, everything higher than the height of a rifle, for example, by the Chetniks. They slaughtered them all. The Chetniks were the Serbs and Montenegrins, so I say the people of Serbia-Montenegro and their army, the then Chetnik Army, entered Eastern Bosnia and slaughtered everyone who was taller than a rifle. And in one day, 84 of my family members were slaughtered. And the village itself has 300 households, so you can imagine what that was, and the people remember that very well. And this is one of the causes of what happened later on. It is cause and effect, and it's been going on for hundreds of years. The Serbs are constantly carrying out genocide against the Muslim people, especially in Eastern Bosnia, because everything has to -- if you -- all the armies have to cross at the Drina River. In order to attack Croatia and Bosnia, they have to go through Eastern Bosnia, and that's the crux of the problem. That is why we placed the emphasis on supplying Eastern Bosnia with weapons. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, for your answer. Thank you, Your Honours. I do believe I have clarified issues somewhat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Petkovic has no questions for this witness. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, 1D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. We have no questions for the gentleman, but we do wish to thank him for coming here and giving his evidence. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Prosecutor, your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will have some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness kindly be asked to slow down when he answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- the interpreters were asking whether you could slow down in giving your answers, because they will have to interpret everything, and if you speak very fast it's difficult for them to interpret. So if you could listen carefully to my questions and answer slowly, please. General, you were asked a number of questions by the Defence of weapon supplies for the BH Army which went through the Logistical Centre in Grude and which were destined for places such as Sarajevo, Foca, Gorazde, Trnovo, and Visegrad. And you were reviewed two orders from the Croatian assistant minister of the defence, Mr. Ivan Cermak, dated the 10th and the 16th of October, 1992, in which weapons were -- and ammunition were put at the disposal of the BiH army in the regions of Foca, Gorazde, Trnovo, and Visegrad. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that these weapons and material for these regions were all intended for the war of the ABiH-HVO alliance against the common enemy, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, that MTS was intended for the Eastern Bosnia Operative Group, and from Grude they came in via Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, and Mount Igman and Trnovo, to the Logistics Base at Grebak, and that base is about some 30 to 40 kilometres away from Sarajevo, under Mount Jahorina. And from thence, the people -- 5.000 people during the night would take one or two rifles, 200 or 300 rounds of ammunition, so that the Eastern Bosnia Operative Group could be armed. And that base survived --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Listen carefully to the questions. A lot of my questions can just be answered by "yes" or "no," and I have a limited amount of time, I only have half an hour. So I would ask you simply if a question can be answered by "yes" or "no," that you would answer it that way. Is it correct that these weapons were used for fighting the VRS Army, the Serbs, this MTS and the weapons that came from Grude?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you also reviewed two other orders which came from the Ministry of Defence from the Republic of Croatia for the distribution of MTS for the BiH forces in Sarajevo in March 1993. Those are documents 2D00311 and 2D008 -- no, 3D0008. Sir, is it correct that these materials and resources from Croatia were also intended for the defence of Sarajevo and the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but, Your Honours, I would like the Prosecutor to allow the witness to take a look at the documents, because I think that that is not what the documents say. So it would be in order if the Prosecutor were to show the documents. It doesn't say "for the defence of the city of Sarajevo" there, it says "for the BH Army," so I don't think that the witness can answer fully unless he is allowed to view the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you reviewed the evidence just a while ago. Can you tell us, what were -- for what purpose were these weapons procured?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I had another document in front of me, but let me answer. All the documents that I looked through, and what it says in those documents, the MTS which was sent through the Logistics Base at Zagreb, or Grude, or down there from Ploce, were given to the BH Army for them to fight the Serbs, and they were used for that purpose. Everything that arrived in Gorazde was used against the Serbs, because there weren't any HVO units for us to fight against the Croats or anybody else. The only people we were fighting against was the Serbs. And the same thing applies to Sarajevo. In Sarajevo itself, I was in command of part of the defence of Sarajevo, the old part, that is to say, the Stari Grad municipality, where I worked, and we were directly facing the Army of Republika Srpska that set up a siege, and of course the weapons were used against the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That answers my question. Let's move on to another topic, and you can leave the document. Sir, is it correct that around -- around the autumn of 1992, that tensions started to surface between the Croats and the Muslims in regions such as Central Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Sarajevo myself. I was the commander of the units over there, those four brigades that were in my area of responsibility, so that I was engaged in that part, as far as defence is concerned. I was not in the General Staff, and I did not know what was happening in other areas of the theatre. But according to the information that reached me, I know that there were certain tensions and that relations were strained. But regardless of that, throughout the time we did have weapons coming in to us from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So -- but you said you learned from information that certain tensions arose between these groups, and did you learn about incidents that occurred in, for example, Novi Travnik and in Prozor in 1992, and later on in January 1992 in Gornji Vakuf; did you learn about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: At the time, there was no information media in Sarajevo, no television, no newspapers. We, the commanders, were informed from the General Staff. That's where our information reached us, through the regular routes that the General Staff applies to BH units. And, of course, every day we knew where the low-intensity conflicts took place along the defence lines. So I knew about those in part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to get back to the beginning, when the Prosecutor, Mr. Bos, put questions to you and said to you that you were the commander of four brigades in Sarajevo. In line with all these questions which are very complex, I shall make the following assumption: If Croatia, via the HVO, had not provided you with weapons in Sarajevo, what would have happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, lots of things would have happened. Well, the whole defence of Sarajevo and the region around it would have come into question, so you've posed a very good question, what would have happened. All sorts of things would have happened. It would be very debatable as to whether we could put up a defence at all or do anything at all. And it would be very difficult to defend Sarajevo without the weapons that arrived through Croatia, because we didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. If you had not had these weapons, what would the Serbs have done? The Serbs would have taken control of Sarajevo or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we didn't have those weapons, we wouldn't have been able to defend ourselves. That's for sure, if there hadn't been any weapons. So the key to the defence of Sarajevo was the 1.000 rifles I brought in from Tihomir Majic. That was the first substantial quantity of weapons placed at the disposal of Sarajevo for its defence, and then through Rogatica, Gorazde, Visegrad, and Grude and so on, that route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question on what Judge Antonetti just asked you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it correct, around that time in 1993, that there were still 30.000 Bosnian Croats living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Whether it was 30.000 -- well, maybe more, because Sarajevo was one of the largest cities of Croatians. It was the largest Serb town and Croatian town, in addition to the Muslims, and most of the Croats stayed on in Sarajevo throughout the war. They would leave from time to time and come back unimpeded. They would go to Croatia unimpeded and come back. And this went on during the whole war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: General, could I ask you to look at a document in the exhibit binder that you have been given, and it's Exhibit P10879.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an article from the "Boston Globe," dated the 23rd of November, 1992, and it contains an interview with the HVO president, Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you have the exhibit in front of you? It's P10879.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Just the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that at least the Prosecutor would try to establish first whether the witness was in the position to see that article while he was there. There is no sense -- there is no any value in evidence if the witness will comment on US press at that time, since he was in Sarajevo, completely under blockade. And by the way, Your Honour, this is for us a new document. We haven't saw it on Rule 65 list or anywhere else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, why is this article not on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I need to put the exhibits that I use in cross for a witness on a 65 ter list, and this -- and I intend to use this exhibit to elicit from this witness how the Bosnian Muslims viewed the situation in late 1992, early 1993, and in particular the Muslims in Sarajevo. That's the reason why I'm showing this document, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, let's not waste time with needless objections. It's quite clear that the witness has not seen this article, but it might be interesting for everyone to see what this article contains and whether this could be of any interest at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, when the Prosecutor was responding, it appears that he is offering a view of the Muslims, if I understood correctly. It is not the view of the Muslims in this article, it is other view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: General, you have the article in front of you? I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the article, and I'm going to ask you a few questions about some of the paragraphs that are listed here in this article. Let me first direct your attention to the fifth paragraph of the article, starting -- the article is an interview with Mr. Boban, who was at the time in Grude, and the fifth article, let me read it out to you, and I'll ask you a question about it. The author here of the article gives a description of Grude: "There are no border posts, passport controls or customs when you cross the border from Croatia, nor is the fleur-de-lis flag of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be seen. It is the red checkered Croatian flag that flies here and over most of the other towns under the control of the Croatian Defence Council, as the Croatian Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina is called. Some of the town names have been changed to reflect Croatian names as well." Now, sir, you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Excuse me. This is not a quote. This is the author's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- viewpoint. Hold on. That's the viewpoint, so what -- so this is -- has nothing to do with Mr. Boban. This is what a journalist saw at that period of time, and if exactly he saw it because we don't have this. Now, I object to this because we don't have this gentleman here. I further object to this -- to going into this evidence, because I understand there is this free evaluation of the evidence, but it seems that when the Defence tries to do that, we get shut down by the Trial Chamber. So I would like equal treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you know that this document will not be tendered into evidence. However, you are right, this is the viewpoint of the journalist. You're quite right. But what may be of interest to everyone is what Mr. Boban "may have said," quote/unquote. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, just on this particular issue, the witness went to Grude as well, although it was in an earlier time in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: My question to the witness is this: When you were in Grude, how did you perceive the town of Grude? Was it a completely Croatian-controlled town, in the way it's been described here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must -- perhaps the gentleman isn't aware of the population makeup in Grude. I think that's part of the -- that's part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm just asking for the witness's impression --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's like going to Greece and saying, "Did you find Greeks there?" Of course you're going to find Greeks. That's where you're going to find them. Same thing in Grude. You're going to find the population is there. Who is -- who populates that area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the witness has been to Grude, and maybe he saw that there were no border posts, he saw that there were flags, he saw perhaps what the journalist saw. Maybe he doesn't remember; maybe he does remember. Mr. Bos, ask him the question so that you can elicit what you want, if he remembers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and how my recollection serves me well, thank God. I arrived in Grude. That day at about midday, I arrived in this town which at the time, as all the other towns, was free of soldiers. There were no flags, no check-points. I came there unhindered. I wasn't checked on the way or inspected. I arrived in Grude municipality, and I was told to report there. I asked to speak to Mr. Tihomir Majic. The janitor said, He's over at the playground. I went to the playground. Tiho Majic, who is Tiho Majic, they told me who he was. I came to get this and that, and he got a couple of men from the playground to help me carry this, because I had only arrived with two other men and two trucks to help me load these items. That's how it was. It was all perfectly open at the time. There were no clashes going on, no restraints being placed on us by the Croats. I arrived the same way I would have in Gorazde or Sarajevo or any other town at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you specify again when exactly you were in Grude, what day?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I arrived on the 26th of February, 1992, at about midday. Actually, I had made Grude at about 3.00. It was after business hours of the town hall, and that's when I reached Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move on a bit further in the article, the third paragraph after the paragraph that we've just looked at. It discusses the referendum which was held also around that same time in February 1992. Do you recall the referendum being held in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, General? Just say "yes" or "no". Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read out this paragraph about the referendum. This is what the article says: "The Croatian minority, however, voted with the Muslims for independence for Yugoslavia, but Croatian acceptance of a new republic and minority status in a unitary state does not mean that Croats in this land plan to give up what they see as their rights to a separate and distinct ethnic community. At times, they have seemed on the verge of setting up their own state too." Sir, an impression -- what was your impression of the Croatian Community at the time? It says here that, you know, at the time they seemed to be on the verge of setting up their own state. Is that something that you thought was also the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. This time, I would like to raise an objection. This is about some statements made by my learned friend Mr. Bos suggesting that the Croats accepted the status of a minority in the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is simply not true. We've been trying for three years here to prove that the Croats wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to be structured as a state belonging to three constituent peoples on perfectly equal terms. That is why I would like to ask my learned friend Mr. Bos to just purify his question and eliminate everything that might be open to challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the transcript. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So based on your personal contacts with the Bosnian Croats in 1992, how would you comment on this statement that has been made here in this article? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This paragraph that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, no comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise to my colleague Mr. Bos, but this is entirely inappropriate, for Mr. Praljak to be speaking in his language while the witness is giving his testimony, and he should be admonished not to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comments, please, Mr. Praljak, because you may influence the witness. I don't know what you said in your language. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't making any comments. I just wanted to make a suggestion to my lawyers. Mr. Bos was talking about the independence of the Muslims, the referendum on the independence of the Muslims in Yugoslavia. No, it was about the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that is misstated. It should have said "Bosnia-Herzegovina," not "Yugoslavia." It's off our screens now, so I was just making the suggestion for that correction to be entered. I wasn't making any suggestions, as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, the referendum was held so that there was a vote on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. And I hope that finally now the witness can answer my question, and I'll repeat the question one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: General, based on your personal contacts with the Bosnian Croats at that time in 1992, how would you comment on the statement made in this article, that even though the Croats voted in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there were times that they seemed to be on the verge of setting up their own state too? What is your comment on this particular statement in the article?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Talking about this paragraph and the article in general, I'm no politician, I'm a soldier. I'm not involved in this kind of thing. Nevertheless, I have the impression that the Croats were not trying to set up their own state within Bosnia and Herzegovina. They would have been practically unable to do anything like that, simply because the Croats are scattered all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not a homogeneous group or a homogeneous territory where they could set up a state. They were fighting for something entirely different. They were fighting for equal rights within Bosnia and Herzegovina, something that would have been considered normal in any state. They sought to attain that sort of a status, not to end up as a minority or not to end up being out-voted all the time, which is a perfectly normal thing to seek.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may comment. Now we see how meaningless it is to use the words of an American journalist, or an American article, dating back to the time in question. If my learned friend wanted to raise the question of the referendum, first of all, it is then a well-known fact. Secondly, there are hundreds and thousands of documents about that. The choice should have been more carefully considered. Maybe a news piece that was written and published in Bosnia at the time, it would have been easier for us to discuss it. This answer shows how entirely meaningless it is to be using an article like this. Now that I've read it, it's really unrelated to anything at all. We've been talking here for the last three years about most of these things, and you, Your Honours, should know that this is entirely meaningless and unrelated to anything that we should be looking at. This is a waste of time, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor, however, is entitled to develop his case in line with the indictment, and the witness answered to the contrary. That is what I have noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- [In English] I want to say of course he has that right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- that, but I'm merely trying to say there is no reason to put the question to the witness and to confront him with so-called facts which are found in this -- in this case, in an American newspaper article. There is nothing realistic there, while at the same time we have so many contemporary documents prepared in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So if he wants to use something, go ahead, use it, but not this kind of press. This doesn't help. This is not a fact. And now, since we finished that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, we have already addressed this issue when we were dealing with the article written by Mr. Sudetic in the American press, print press. We had the same problem then. The Prosecution is relying on articles to develop its case, and the Bench will assess the probative value of all of this at the end of the case. Anyway, the witness has answered the question. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. General, could I ask you to look at another document, which is P10864. This is an article from the "Boston Globe," and it describes the situation in Sarajevo around March 1993. And, in fact, it describes the confrontation line in the area where the HVO is defending. And I'll ask you to put your attention to about the seventh paragraph starting from the top, and let me read out what's being said here: "The fighters here are ethnic Croats from the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: "The fighters here are ethnic Croats from the HVO, known here by the initials of the HVO in the Serbo-Croatian language. Like the rest of Sarajevo's defenders, the HVO's 2.000 men are hanging by the skin of their teeth. With a minimum of weapons and without proper uniforms, they are trying to hold one of the most sensitive and dangerous stretches of the front in the very centre of Sarajevo. If the Serbs break through, they will be less than a mile from the Bosnian seat of government and the military high command." Sir, does this article and the paragraphs that I just read out give an accurate description of what the defence situation was in Sarajevo in March 1993 for both the Muslims and the Croat forces who were trying to defend the city?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: The distribution is accurate, essentially. That's what it was like. There were about 2.000 HVO soldiers in Sarajevo, a brigade, briefly. It had its own area of responsibility, and it was unarmed, unequipped, the same as all the other units defending Sarajevo. It is true that it was just across the river from the Presidency and the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the distance between those buildings and this being several hundred metres, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me continue more towards the end of this article, and I'm going to read out a few more paragraphs to you from this article. About seven or eight paragraphs down from what we just read out: "In theory, Bosnia and its western neighbour, Croatia, are allies in the battle against Serbia's Slobodan Milosevic to builder a Greater Serbia, but the alliance is shaky. Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, who can seem moderate only when measured against Milosevic, makes no efforts to hide his plans to grab 'hums' of Western Bosnia. A book of maps published recently in the Croatian capital Zagreb fails to mention Bosnia in the list of countries with which it has a common border. The official leaders of Bosnian Croats party are viewed here as Tudjman puppets and now live in Zagreb. HVO forces in Western Bosnia already control far more land than they would be given under the Vance-Owen -- the Cyrus Vance-David Owen Peace Plan, and there have been clashes between HVO and Bosnian armed forces in the west of the republic." Sir, was this the type of news that would be read -- or that people in Sarajevo would learn about Franjo Tudjman, that he was trying to grab "hums" of Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: It's true that President Izetbegovic and Mr. Franjo Tudjman created an alliance of sorts in order to fight the Serbs. The alliance existed throughout the war. We were receiving technical and material assistance from Croatia throughout the war, which to a large extent helped us to not be overcome and not lose everything that we were fighting for. There were some things that were said here, and there is this book. I know nothing about either of these. Therefore, I can't say anything. I haven't read the book; I can't comment. It is true that there were clashes in Western Bosnia. Nevertheless, the clashes were limited. They were local clashes and had no significant influence on the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement. As for these maps and all that, I am unaware of that. I've never had a chance to look at these, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just read out the last paragraph of this -- of this article.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly indicate where the paragraph is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It continues from where I stopped. It's the last three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: "But Sarajevo is a remarkable melting pot, where the ethnic groups are intermarried and intermingled, and at least 6.000 Serbs have voluntarily stayed on throughout the siege. "Bosnian Croats are also prominent in the war effort. The special police is commanded by a Bosnian Croat, Dragan Vikic. He makes it clear his loyalty does not lie in Croatia. "'I couldn't live in Zagreb,' Vikic said. 'I have a different accent and a different approach to life.'" Sir, do you know who Dragan Vikic was?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I know very well who he is. He's a friend of mine. He was a commander of a special unit comprising about 200 men in Sarajevo. They were living and working in Sarajevo, and they were fighting in order to defend Sarajevo. He's a legend of the city's defence, you might say. He says he couldn't live in Zagreb. He was born in Sarajevo, and he loves his native town. That applies to most people, regardless of any other statements that he may or may not have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's almost quarter to 4.00. May we have the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have the break now. You must have something like ten minutes or so left. I don't know. The Registrar will give us the countdown. We shall resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you have eight minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: General, could I ask you, by whom were you contacted to appear as a witness for the Defence of Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this line of questioning. I would object to this line of questioning. I think it has a chilling effect when we begin asking witnesses who contacted them. We are free to contact any witness, "we" being the Defence, free to contact witnesses, and I think it's totally inappropriate. I would like to know what the relevance of this question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The relevance will come, but I'm happy to rephrase the question if it's considered a chilling question. I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, the effect is chilling, so I would like to know the relevance. What is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, at this point. We don't hear the question and the answer and then determine what the relevance is. I'd like to know, what is this -- why is this relevant? I'm posing an objection. I would like an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if somebody is to raise an objection, it should be Ms. Nozica. He's her witness, not yours. So you're just -- it's not your own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. President, because when we don't object, when we don't do things, we get accused of not being due diligent, and I'm quoting -- I'm quoting the Trial Chamber now. We get accused of not being due diligent. My responsibility is to be due diligent for my client, and that is exactly what I'm doing. That's why I'm entitled to object, and I've made an objection. I'm entitled to hear a response, and I'm entitled to a ruling. It is not sufficient for you to say it's in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have a decision. Ms. Nozica, the question put by the Prosecutor, is that a problem for you or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question is problematic on the general level, and there I agree absolutely with my colleague Mr. Karnavas. It is not Ms. Nozica's witness, it is a witness of the Stojic Defence. Now, because I know what the Prosecutor wants to elicit through this question, because I know why the Prosecutor is asking the question, in fact, I consider that even if the witness were to answer the question, the witness will explain what kind of contact he had. But the Prosecutor mustn't forget the fact that the Defence of Mr. Stojic came into possession of a document with this witness's name there, and he was selected because his name is on a document and because he was involved in an operation, as we saw during the examination-in-chief, and that is the sole reason why he was chosen, not for any other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After discussing the issue, we decide that the question can be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So I'll repeat the question, General. By whom were you contacted to appear as a witness for the Defence of Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I was contacted by friends, by my friends from Western Herzegovina, and Senka Nozica, when they came into possession of a document that I signed for the procurement of weapons for the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was this the first time that you spoke to Ms. Senka Nozica about -- or had you known Ms. Nozica before?

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: Well, I've known Senka for 50 years, for as long as I've lived. I've always known who Senka Nozica was. She lived and grew up in Sarajevo, and we know each other from before and from some other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Right. Let me just ask you a question about some of the other cases. Is it correct, sir, that Ms. Nozica was your Defence counsel in 2002, in relation to a criminal case where you and a number of other people were accused of weapons smuggling to Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question I expected to be asked has been asked. Now it's up to you whether you're going to decide whether you're going to allow these questions being responded to. I have -- I'm a lawyer. I have no problem with being Defence counsel for anyone, but that has nothing to do with these proceedings, with this trial, nor could the Prosecutor prove otherwise, because it has absolutely nothing to do with this. If he is trying to discredit the witness because I did my work professionally, then I consider that to be completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the fact that Ms. Nozica was your Defence lawyer, as has been alleged by the Prosecutor, that is part and parcel of the sacrosanct rights of confidentiality, the privileged relationship between you and your lawyer. If you believe that this would jeopardise this privileged communication, you may not answer, but if that's fine with you, you can answer. Did you understand our decision? Mr. Bos, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not -- I do not have too many questions about, you know, what these proceedings were for. I was just told that this information was relevant for the Trial Chamber to know, and I do not intend to go into detail about what this case was about and -- I just wanted to mention the mere fact that this incident occurred, and I will hereby conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica, do you have redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just linked to this last question, I'd like to ask the witness a few questions after that. We don't need to go into private session. What I'm going to ask the witness can be asked in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bahto, your decision to come in and testify in this trial, was it our professional relationship that influenced that decision and the fact that I was Defence counsel for you on one occasion, or because you and I have known each other for 50 years, or did you decide to come in and be a witness to confirm what happened in 1992 and 1993? And just briefly answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMID BAHTO
utterances.text: I came here voluntarily, of my own free will, without coercion from anyone, and I came to testify to the advantage of the man who helped the army and my people during 1992 and 1993. So that was the only reason that I came here. It was because Bruno Stojic -- of Bruno Stojic and Tihomir Majic who took part with me in the arming of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
